lessons.title: दोपहर (dopahar) — the same word, a wider job than its etymology promised
lessons.gloss: "afternoon" — the same word already met meaning precisely "noon" (two pahars after sunrise, HI-C17), now widened in modern everyday usage to cover the whole afternoon stretch, not just the exact midday moment

segments.text: You already know दोपहर (dopahar) means "noon" — two pahars after sunrise, precisely. This lesson's honest twist is that the word doesn't stay that precise in everyday use.

blocks.title: You'll want to know — दोपहर — same word, a broader modern meaning

segments.text: दोपहर (dopahar) is the exact word you met in Chapter 17, still literally "two pahars" (traditional 3-hour watches, counted from sunrise) — but in modern, everyday Hindi, it no longer points only at that precise midday instant. Say दोपहर में (dopahar mein, "in the dopahar") to arrange a meeting, and you're pointing at a stretch of time — roughly noon through late afternoon — not a single moment. The historical etymology gave the word a very specific target (the end of the second daytime pahar); everyday usage has since widened that target into the general block of time most languages call "the afternoon."

blocks.title: You'll want to know — Be honest: etymology and modern meaning have drifted apart

segments.text: This is worth sitting with: दोपहर (dopahar)'s literal story still holds up the way Chapter 17 described it — "two pahars," with noon falling around the end of the second — though, as that lesson itself noted, treat the exact pahar-count as the general shape of the story rather than a precisely dated fact. Either way, the word's job in the language has moved on well past that etymology. This kind of drift — a word for one precise instant loosening into a name for a whole surrounding stretch of time — isn't unique to Hindi, but here it's especially visible because Chapter 17 showed you exactly how tight the original math was.

segments.text: Is दोपहर (dopahar) a new word, or the same one from Chapter 17? (The same word — "two pahars.") Does modern Hindi use दोपहर (dopahar) to mean only the exact instant of noon? (No — it's widened to cover the whole afternoon, roughly noon through late afternoon.) Has दोपहर (dopahar)'s etymology itself changed to match this wider modern use? (No — the etymology still points precisely at noon; only the word's everyday job has widened.)

lessons.title: ज (ja) — a letter you have been reading without being taught
lessons.gloss: the single character ज — on the page since the second chapter and never once drawn for you

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
waitUntilStopped: Script: where it has been hiding
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ज, Script: where it has been hiding and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ए — does it sit on a consonant or stand alone?
This next one is not new to your eye. It is new to your hand.
ज — ja.
What it is made of:
an open left hook curling clockwise around the lower bowl and continuing through the middle bar.
a top-to-bottom right stem.
the top shirorekhā.

blocks.title: Script: where it has been hiding

segments.text: You have been reading this letter for a long time without anyone stopping to name it:
जी — the respect-marker in जी हाँ.
जनवरी — January, and जून and जुलाई after it.

That is worth saying out loud rather than passing over. A letter can appear on every other page and still never be taught, because the words that carry it were introduced for their meanings and the shapes inside them were left to look after themselves.
Seeing a shape often is not the same as being shown it. The first gives you a guess; the second gives you the letter.

1. start at the open upper-left tip, sweep down and clockwise around the lower bowl, then rise through the inner shoulder and continue right along the middle bar to the right-stem junction without lifting.
2. lift and draw the right stem top-to-bottom.
3. lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right.
Pen lifts: 2. The pen comes up 2 times and no more.
Verified three-stroke teaching form fitted to the bundled printed outline; everyday handwriting may divide the hook and bar differently.

This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Opiaterein, ‘Deva-ज (ja)-order.gif’, strokes 1–3, Wikimedia Commons, 10 May 2009.
